tools.name: load_rom
tools.description: Load a Game Boy cartridge from a file path and start it from cold. Replaces whatever was running. Returns the cartridge title and whether structured game state is available for it (Pokémon Red/Blue only; every other cartridge still supports screenshot, read_memory, press_buttons and step).

model.description: Console to run it on. Default auto: read the cartridge's CGB flag.

tools.name: reset
tools.description: Reboot the current cartridge from cold, as the console's power switch does. Battery-backed save data survives; save states and anything in RAM do not.

tools.name: observe
tools.description: Read the game's state as structured data: what the game is doing (title/overworld/dialogue/menu/battle/cutscene), the text currently on screen with what shape of screen it is (screen.kind: no-text/text/dialogue/menu/yes-no/naming-keyboard), the item the menu cursor points at (screen.selected), whether the decode can be trusted (screen.trust — anything but 'ok' means screen.text was withheld rather than guessed), and whether it is waiting for a button. Sprites — people and objects — are drawn over the tilemap and are NOT in screen.text. For Pokémon Red/Blue it also returns the player's map, coordinates and facing, the map's exits, party, badges, money and the battle opponent. Prefer this over screenshot: it is a few hundred bytes where an image is orders of magnitude more, and it is the only way to tell whether an action worked.

tools.name: screenshot
tools.description: The current frame as a PNG image. Use it when there is no address or structured field for what you need to know — an unfamiliar cartridge, a graphical puzzle, or confirming what the player would actually see. It does not advance time.

scale.description: Nearest-neighbour upscale of the 160x144 frame. 1 is smallest; 2-3 is easier to read at 4-9x the size.

tools.name: read_memory
tools.description: Read bytes of the Game Boy's address space (0x0000-0xFFFF) exactly as the CPU would see them, without perturbing timing. This is what makes an agent fast: one read of a known address beats inferring the same fact from pixels. Returns hex and decimal.

address.description: Start address. Accepts a number; write hex as decimal (0xD35E = 54110).

tools.name: press_buttons
tools.description: Press buttons with exact frame timing and run the machine until the press has finished, so state read straight afterwards reflects it. Works on any cartridge. Use this for title screens, menus and anything the higher-level actions do not cover. Buttons in one call are pressed in order, not together.

times.description: Repeat the whole sequence this many times. Default 1.

hold_frames.description: Frames to hold each button. Default 6.

gap_frames.description: Frames of quiet after each press. Default 24 - Pokemon's menu code ignores presses closer together than about that.

tools.name: run_actions
tools.description: Run a short plan of high-level actions and report what each one achieved. Pokémon Red/Blue only. This is the tool that keeps a session affordable: 'advance_text' holds a whole conversation down, and 'goto' walks to a coordinate around what blocks it - one call covering hundreds of frames instead of one call per button. Every action is bounded and reports honestly when it was stopped by a wall or a cap.

actions.description: Up to 12 actions, run in order.

do.description: press: tap a button, with 'button' and optional 'times'. walk: take 'steps' steps in 'dir', stopping at a wall. goto: head for 'x','y' on this map. advance_text: press A through dialogue until it ends. wait: do nothing for 'frames'.

tools.name: step
tools.description: Advance the emulator by a number of frames and do nothing else. The game runs at 59.7275 frames a second, so 60 is about one second. Use it to let a boot sequence, a fade or an animation finish, and on cartridges the higher-level actions do not understand.

frames.description: Frames to run. Capped by the server's --max-frames.

tools.name: save_state
tools.description: Snapshot the complete machine to a numbered slot or a file, so a later load_state returns to exactly this point. Slots are namespaced by cartridge and are the same ones the terminal frontend's F5/F8 use.

path.description: Write to this exact file instead of a slot.

tools.name: load_state
tools.description: Restore a snapshot taken by save_state. A state from a different cartridge is refused rather than loaded.

path.description: Read this exact file instead of a slot.

tools.name: render_audio
tools.description: Render Game Boy sound-chip instructions to a WAV file through the emulated APU — the same chip the accuracy suites score, so the answer is what the hardware would produce, not an imitation. Needs no cartridge. Feed it a score (notes, durations, envelopes, duty, sweep, noise), a register script (NR10-NR52 with timings), or the path of a .vgm log. Returns what was produced — length, peak level, which channels sounded — and optionally the compiled register writes, which is the ground truth the audio comes from. You cannot hear the file; use `registers` and the reported levels to check your work, and give the path to a person to listen to. Score syntax: `tempo 120`, then lines like `ch1 duty 2`, `ch1 env 15 - 3`, `ch1 note C4 1/8`, `ch3 wave <32 hex digits>`, `ch4 noise 4 15 4`, `ch4 hit 1/16`, `ch2 rest 1/4`. Each channel keeps its own cursor from time zero, so parts written one after another play together.

score.description: The source text: a score, or a register script. Mutually exclusive with "path".

path.description: Read the source from this file instead. This is the only way to render a .vgm log.

out.description: Where to write the .wav. Default: a file in the system temp directory.

model.description: Which console's APU. A `model` line in the source wins. Default dmg.

registers.description: Include the compiled register writes in the reply. Default false; they can be long.
